name: PT Golden Eagle Energy Tbk

frontmatter.title: Golden Eagle Energy — a low-grade, long-haul thermal producer priced past its cycle
frontmatter.summary: Golden Eagle Energy is a small Indonesian thermal-coal producer whose sub-bituminous coal and long road haul set its realised price at a fraction of the seaborne benchmark. This revision puts the overburden rate back on its disclosed history after the H1 anomaly, strips all amortisation out of the cash cost, and discloses that the price leg follows the deck rather than the H1 print. The target rises modestly; the shares still sit far above our through-cycle value, so SELL holds.
thesis: We stay at SELL with a target of Rp1,323 against a price of Rp2,750, a total return of -51.4%.

The variant view is grade and logistics, not price direction: Triaryani's coal is a sub-bituminous product around 4,100 kcal/kg GAR whose realised price has run at roughly a third of the Newcastle marker, and the road haul to the Lalan terminal is the single largest cost line in the P&L [S3] [S2].

At the coal deck's through-cycle Newcastle marker the realised price covers cash cost by only a thin margin and does not cover sustaining capital, so free cash flow turns slightly negative from FY2029E and the reserve beyond 2030 is worth nothing in the base case [S3] [S4] [F10].
The market is not paying for through-cycle cash flow; today's price requires the seaborne benchmark to run at a multiple of the deck's forward path to be justified [S0].

The price is a regime price, not a fundamental one: at 15.2 times our fundamental value the house konglo lens holds part of that premium for twelve months even now that the HSC exclusion from the IHSG calculation is effective, which is why the target is Rp1,323 against a fundamental value of Rp180 [S0] [S7] [S14].

The bull case is real and we state it: a sustained war-premium bid in seaborne coal, a lifted RKAB quota, a wider third-party sales mix and a renewal of the mine licence past the end of the decade at the disclosed extension prior would together change the arithmetic [S6] [S13].

blocks.text: **Revision, 1 November 2026 — what changed and why.** The QC auditor found the base case had swung from too optimistic on cost to too cautious on stripping, and it was right. Three things change, all fundamental. First, the overburden rate. The H1-2026 charge is real and is carried: the half-year charge of US$11.5m is more than the whole of last year's US$8.2m, so FY2026E keeps a full-year charge built from the H1 actual plus a second-half estimate on last year's seasonal split, which is a 5.3 bcm/t annual average [S4 note 28] [F43] [F44]. But that average already embeds a second half back near the FY2025 rate, and it is not a mine plan. No mine plan, work plan/RKAB, presentation or public expose in the archive states an annual BCM rate [S2 p.81, p.99] [S6]; the disclosed overburden volumes over production give the last audited year a ratio at the top of the three-year range [F10] [S2 p.20]. FY2027E-FY2030E and the long-run tail therefore revert to the sourced FY2025 ratio of 2.9 bcm/t. That puts FY2028E-FY2030E EBITDA back in positive territory, extends the value-maximising life from FY2027E to FY2028E and leaves a tail that is still non-positive at the deck's through-cycle marker: the breakeven where EBIT covers sustaining capital sits just above the deck's long-run Newcastle marker, so the extension stays unbooked — now on the arithmetic rather than on a half-year anomaly [d.coal.newc]. Second, the cash cost is on a clean definition: H1 cost of sales less royalty, less the full cost-of-sales depreciation and amortisation line of US$0.7m (not only the PP&E depreciation slice of it), less overburden, gives US$30.0 a tonne rather than the previous higher figure, so no non-cash amortisation is charged again through the model's depreciation line [S4 note 28, note 42]. Third, we disclose that the price leg is not tied to the H1 print: FY2026E ASP follows the deck's full-year marker at the calibrated ratio, while the cost leg is anchored on the H1 actual [S2 p.96] [S4 p.6]. Together these bring FY2026E net profit to US$11.1m, below the company's own US$12.7m plan profit [S2 p.96]. The target moves to **Rp1,323** and the total return to -51.4%; the **SELL** rating is unchanged. The 2 November HSC exclusion from the IHSG calculation is still the dated regime event it was, and the shares remain listed and tradeable [S14] [S15]; it is not a new valuation input.

This note replaces the 27 October 2026 initiation, which was withdrawn while the name was re-run under the house's konglo regime lens. What this revision changes is the overburden rate, the cash-cost definition and the tail, and all three are fundamental. First, the overburden rate now rests on the disclosed history rather than on a half-year print carried for five years: FY2026E carries the H1-incurred charge, and FY2027E-FY2030E carry the FY2025 ratio [F10] [F4]. Second, the cash cost strips the whole cost-of-sales depreciation and amortisation line, so the model's separate depreciation line is not a double charge [S4 note 28, note 42]. Third, the tail: the 314 Mt reserve beyond the 2030 operating permit is still not booked, because on a nominal-consistent path, with price and unit costs escalating together, it is negative at the deck's through-cycle marker even at the sourced strip ratio, so the extension is carried as an unbooked option rather than a filed fact or a bridge item [S13] [d.coal.newc]. Carried from the prior round unchanged: tax at the rate the last audited LK shows being paid [S3]; the netting of the restricted export-proceeds deposit against the bank loan it secures [S4 note 17]; and the mark-down of the associate, whose own permit has expired and which produced nothing this year [S2] [S6]. The realised price — calibrated on a related-party contract — is still stressed in the bear case, but as the mirror of the bull's upgrade rather than an unsourced claim that the related party pays above market [S3]. What the lens adds on top is the regime step. SMMT is a konglo name in the regime sense — the listed vehicle of a Singapore-controlled coal group, on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list, with a free float below the new statutory floor — and the house lens sets the twelve-month target as the fundamental value times the share of today's premium the regime keeps over the window. That is **Rp1,323** against a fundamental value of Rp180, because the price sits at 15.2 times value and the base regime keeps most of that gap rather than closing it. The rating is unchanged at **SELL**: the price is many times what the asset is worth on our own numbers even after the regime step.

We cover PT Golden Eagle Energy Tbk (SMMT) at **SELL** with a twelve-month target of **Rp1,323** versus a last price of Rp2,750, a total return of -51.4%. The company is a small Indonesian thermal-coal producer that sells a sub-bituminous product from one operating concession in South Sumatra and holds an indirect minority in a second mine in East Kalimantan that is operating but idle this year [S2] [S6]. Its coal is low-rank and its mine is a long road haul from the barging terminal, so its realised price ran at roughly a third of the Newcastle benchmark in the last audited year and its cost base is dominated by haulage, barging and jetty handling rather than by the coal-getting itself [S3] [S2]. The company has just re-rated sharply: the shares rose by roughly three-quarters in the month to end-September 2026, the exchange flagged unusual market activity and then suspended trading for cooling down, and management's own incidental public expose attributes the move mainly to transaction volume and to the index price rather than to a change in the business [S5] [S6].

Our variant view is not about the coal price. It is that the market is capitalising this asset on the seaborne benchmark while the company's own realised price is a small fraction of it, and that at the deck's through-cycle marker the realised price covers cash cost by only a thin margin and does not cover sustaining capital, so free cash flow turns slightly negative from FY2029E — even after we strip the one-off development spend that inflated the last two years' capex out of the run rate [S3] [S4] [F10]. Working from that marker, the calibrated realisation and the rate the accounts show being paid in royalty, the life-of-asset DCF is worth only Rp61 against today's price. The three things that move the value are the seaborne benchmark path, the annual RKAB quota that caps volume, and the haulage cost per tonne — the last of which the company has been investing to relieve through its Lalan river terminal and its own barge ports [S2].

We are not bearish by default. The bull case is explicit and is carried in the scenarios: a sustained war-premium bid in seaborne thermal coal, an RKAB quota lifted toward the company's own plan, a wider third-party sales mix and a little more volume would together lift realised price and margin. The licence extension and the associate's restart are separate, dated optionality we carry in the signposts rather than in the scenarios or the bridge. A reader who believes the benchmark stays near spot rather than reverting to the deck should own this name; a reader who believes the deck should not.

Golden Eagle Energy began life as an entertainment company and only moved into coal mining in this
century, taking over a South Sumatran concession that has been producing since the middle of the
last decade. It is controlled by a Singapore-listed coal group whose regional office sits in
Jakarta, and its shares carry a very small free float, which makes the tape thin and prone to large
moves on modest flow. Sub-bituminous Indonesian coal of this rank is sold mainly to power stations
and cement plants in Asia, so demand tracks electricity generation and industrial activity rather
than the steel cycle.

Golden Eagle Energy is a coal-mining holding company. Its product reaches the market through PT Triaryani, a wholly-owned subsidiary that holds an IUP Operasi Produksi over a concession in the Musi Rawas Utara regency of South Sumatra and has been operating since the middle of the last decade [S2]. A second mine, PT Internasional Prima Coal in Palaran, East Kalimantan, is held as a forty-nine per cent associate through PT Mega Raya Kusuma and is therefore equity-accounted rather than consolidated [S2] [S6]. That distinction matters for anyone modelling the group: the income statement carries only Triaryani's revenue, while the group's headline operating statistics in the annual report include the associate's tonnes [S2]. The associate is not a shell: it is an operating mine with a higher-rank product than Triaryani's, holding an IUP over a large concession in East Kalimantan with its own haul road and barging ports [S2]. It produced 0.7 Mt and sold 0.7 Mt in the last audited year and sold close to a million tonnes the year before, and it paid the group US$2.1m of cash dividends in the last audited year [S2] [S3]. What it is is idle: it produced nothing at all in the current year while its licence ran down, and management blames the associate's absence for part of the group's output decline [S6]. So it is a real, cash-generative asset that is switched off, not a dormant one — it sold 0.7 Mt in the last audited year, close to a million tonnes the year before, and paid the group cash dividends US$2.1m [S2] [S3]. It is worth no more than its book in the base case for a specific reason: its IUP Operasi Produksi expired in 2026 [S2], so we mark the stake to its share of the associate's own net assets rather than to the carrying premium the accounts show, and we hold the restart as an unbooked option [S3]. The valuation section sets out that mark-down and the value it removes.

The product is thermal coal, and its rank is the heart of the investment case. Triaryani's coal carries a calorific value of about 4,100 kcal/kg GAR with low sulphur and low ash, and the company's own public-expose material describes the product as clean and homogeneous at a rank in the low four-thousands [S2] [S6]. The associate's coal is a materially higher-rank product [S2]. Both are open-pit operations; the group reports a single reportable segment, coal mining, and a single geographic area, Indonesia, so there is no segment split to manage [S3].

Strategically the company is a capacity builder rather than a consolidator. Its stated levers are to raise the production target inside the annual work plan and budget while respecting the logistics constraint of its coal haul road, to add haulage fleet and improve port loading, and to widen its market through long-term contracts while protecting coal quality to hold the selling price [S2]. The haulage route is the binding constraint: coal travels by road to a terminal on the Lalan river and then barges out, and the company has been adding road, jetty and barge-port infrastructure rather than buying tonnes [S2]. Management has also been restructuring the group's holding chain, moving its stake in the associate through a holding vehicle and buying the remaining interest in one of its intermediate holding companies in the last audited year [S3] [S6].

On competitive position the company is a challenger, not a leader. Its concession is small against the state producer or the large private coal names, it reports a single mine's worth of reserves rather than a portfolio, and it has no metallurgical coal, no downstream smelter and no branded product [S2]. The group employed a small workforce at the last count and has no institutionally-held float to speak of, with public shareholders holding a low-double-digit share of the register and the controlling shareholder holding the balance [S0].

Indonesian thermal coal is a mature, policy-shaped export industry. National production fell in the last completed year, the government's own reference price for high-calorie coal fell by roughly a fifth across that year, and the director general's published expectation for the coming year's national production target is lower again on softer demand from the main export destinations [S2]. Domestic consumption takes a large slice of national output through the domestic market obligation, with the balance exported or carried into stock [S2]. For a producer of this size, the binding constraints are therefore not market share but the annual government work plan and budget, known as the RKAB, which caps how much a concession may produce, and the US dollar reference prices the government sets twice a month [S2] [S6].

The coal deck is the driver we underwrite against. Its reviewed marker for high-rank seaborne thermal coal is a forecast path that starts above the last realised year, steps down through the middle of the decade and settles at a long-run level, with the deck explicitly flagging that spot sits well above the forward path as a war-premium carry rather than a level it expects to persist US$137/t US$118/t US$105/t. The government's own high-calorie reference price and the domestic power cap bracket the product set, and the deck's lower-rank reference prices for mid- and low-calorie grades show how steeply value declines with rank US$127/t US$70.0/t US$66.1/t. The deck's read on Indonesia's supply discipline and the demand outlook is the backdrop we work to [S2].

That grade ladder is our whole competitive read. A producer at the top of the rank ladder can realise close to the seaborne benchmark; a producer at Triaryani's rank realises a fraction of it, and then hands a further slice of the delivered price to the road haul, the barge, the jetty and the transshipment step before the coal reaches a vessel [S3]. Coal of this rank also competes with domestic mine-mouth supply for the power plants, and the domestic market obligation caps what those tonnes can earn at the government's power price rather than at export parity [S2].

On the five forces, buyer concentration is the practical constraint: a very large share of group revenue is a sale to a single related party within the controlling shareholder's group, under a coal sales and purchase agreement alongside a marketing-services agreement with the same counterparty [S3]. Suppliers are fewer than they look, because much of the cost base is contracted haulage and barging rather than a competitive commodity input [S3]. Related-party gravity runs through the cost side as well as the revenue side, and round one understated it. The logistics that carry the largest cost line — the haul road and the jetty — are provided by PT Marga Bara Jaya, an affiliate of the same controlling group, and the group funds that build through advances booked as other non-current assets [S3 note 17, note 34]. On the accounts' own cost-of-sales split, hauling is US$48.0m and jetty and loading a further US$8.0m [S3 note 28], together the majority of the cost of sales, so a large part of the cost base is contracted with an entity inside the controlling shareholder's group. Read the other way, the marketing-services fee the same group charges on the sales side, US$1.8m, is under a dollar a tonne off the realised price [S3 note 29, note 34]. We are precise about what is disclosed and what is not: the filing does not name the counterparty of the haulage charge line itself, and the one supplier it discloses above a tenth of sales is a third party [S3 note 28], so the related-party cost exposure is real but cannot be sized to the last dollar from the notes. A member of the board is also the president director of that logistics affiliate, which we note as a governance fact rather than a financing one [S2]. Barriers to entry are high on paper, since mining permits are not freely available, but they protect an incumbent that is still subscale and high-cost, which is a weak moat in practice [S2]. Substitution risk over the long run comes from the energy transition, which the company itself flags as its central sustainability challenge, and from the electrification of the mine fleet it says it is exploring [S2]. Regulation is the swing force: royalties, the domestic market obligation, export-proceeds retention rules and the frequency with which the RKAB quota is reset all move the economics of a marginal tonne more than they move a first-quartile one [S2] [S6].

The last audited year was a year of growth with almost no margin. Consolidated revenue doubled, but cost of sales rose by nearly the same amount, so gross profit was only a thin slice of sales and operating profit was marginal once general and administrative costs were taken 103.6 95.2 8.4 4.3. Reported net profit was small but larger than operating profit, because the group's share of the associate's earnings, a foreign-exchange gain and interest income all sat below the operating line [S3]. The cost of sales note is the most revealing page in the filing: haulage alone is the largest line, followed by barging, overburden removal, jetty and loading, then depreciation and amortisation, then the government royalty [S3]. Coal-getting proper is a minor item. This is a logistics business with a mine attached.

Volume is the swing factor, and the reported series is volatile. Triaryani sold roughly a million tonnes two years ago, then around two and a half million in the last audited year, and the company's own plan for the current year names a volume target well above that, paired with a revenue target that implies a materially higher realised price [S2]. We do not carry that plan into the base case, but not on the grounds round one used. Round one justified the gap with the claim that the company "met its own published plans at only a majority-of-target rate in each year it discloses"; that is only half supported and its locator was wrong. The annual report states in one place that the last audited year's production plan was met at 65.0% of the target set at the start of the year [S2], while its own structured target table shows the same year's sales target for Triaryani met at 2.5 Mt against 2.6 Mt actually sold — the target was reached, not missed [S2]. Two figures in one document, so we refuse to lean on either. The base case instead anchors on the hard print: group sales of 1.3 Mt in the first half with no production at all from the associate, blamed on a work-plan quota issued only at the end of March [S4] [S6]. Annualising that run-rate and allowing a modest second-half recovery gives 2.7 Mt, rising only to 2.9 Mt and 3.0 Mt on paper. The comparison is like-for-like: 2.7 Mt is about a twentieth above the consolidated FY2025 actual of 2.6 Mt, not below the group's 0.7 Mt plus Triaryani total, which adds an associate that is idle this year [S2 p.81]. We state that plainly rather than present the base as conservative. The company's 5.5 Mt plan is rejected for volume because it needs second-half sales more than three times the first-half print; its US$250.2m revenue plan implies a price below what the company actually realised in H1, so we do not adopt the plan's margin either [S2 p.96] [S4 p.6].

The profit reconciliation is where this revision moves the base year. H1-2026 net profit to parent was US$3.8m on revenue of US$61.6m, a mid-single-digit net margin, and the cost-of-sales note shows why: other cash cost per tonne ran at US$30.0 against FY2025's lower rate, with overburden and hauling the two largest lines [S4 p.6, note 28]. The stripping line is the one that needed the closest read: the half-year charge of US$11.5m is more than the whole of last year's US$8.2m, so we take a full-year charge of the H1 actual plus a second-half estimate built on last year's seasonal split, which is 5.3 bcm/t at the last audited cost per bcm [F43] [F44] [S4 note 28]. That rate is the annual average of a half-year print, not a mine plan, so only FY2026E carries it; the later years use the disclosed FY2025 ratio, discussed below. Carrying that cost base, the calibrated realisation and the LK tax rate gives FY2026E net profit of US$11.1m — below the company's own US$12.7m plan profit, on roughly half its volume, so the plan's better price and heavier volumes more than offset our cost base [S2 p.96] [S3]. We do not force the model to the plan's profit either way: its volume and price are not separable from its margin, and at the H1-2026 cost base the plan's stated profit no longer implies a better-than-plan margin.

Realisation is the second swing factor and the one the market seems to ignore. We calibrate it on the last actual rather than on a forecast year, dividing the realised consolidated price by the benchmark's own average for the same year, so the ratio carries Triaryani's rank discount and its delivered-logistics point without any additional haircut: a ratio of 0.37, being US$103.6m of revenue over 2.6 Mt sold [S3] [S2]. That ratio, applied to the deck's through-cycle marker, is what produces a through-cycle realised price in the high thirties of dollars per tonne 39.1.

The price leg is not tied to the H1 print, unlike the cost leg, and we state that plainly. FY2026E ASP of US$51.0 follows the deck's full-year Newcastle path at the calibrated ratio, which sits above the H1 realised price implied by US$61.6m of revenue over 1.3 Mt. The implied second-half price is the full-year ASP on 2.7 Mt less the H1 revenue, spread over the second-half tonnes, so it is above the H1 print as well. There is no contractual pass-through that would make the second half track the first, and the bear and bull shocks hit this same path by mirrored amounts, so the asymmetry is disclosed rather than buried [d.coal.newc] [S4 p.6] [S6 p.11].

On costs we hold the cost per cubic metre of overburden and the D&A rate at the last audited year in real terms, and calibrate the other cash cost to the H1-2026 print. Other cash cost is US$30.0 a tonne — H1 cost of sales less royalty, less the whole cost-of-sales depreciation and amortisation line, less overburden, over H1 sales — rather than FY2025's lower figure, so the definition is genuinely cash and the model's separate depreciation line is not a double charge [S4 note 28, note 42] [F46]. The strip ratio is 5.3 bcm/t in FY2026E, then the disclosed FY2025 ratio of 2.9 bcm/t in FY2027E-FY2030E: the half-year charge of US$11.5m at the last audited cost per cubic metre implies roughly the whole of a prior year's stripping in six months, so the H1-incurred cost is carried in the current year, but the model's own second half is already back near the historical rate and no mine plan or work plan in the filings sets an annual BCM schedule [S2 p.20, p.81] [S6]. Holding the H1 average for five years would be an unsourced step, not conservatism; holding the disclosed ratio is the sourced path. This replaces the previous draft's inference that the doubled charge was timing ahead of second-half production, which was ours rather than the filing's, and it also replaces the round-two response that carried the H1 average indefinitely [F43] [F44]. Carrying the cost base gives a full-year unit cash cost of US$36.1 a tonne against a depreciation rate of US$2.1 [S4 note 28]. Royalty is set at the effective rate the accounts show being paid rather than at the tiered schedule, because the paid rate is stable across the last two audited years and the schedule's bands bracket it rather than match it 7.9% [S3]. Tax is the rate the last audited LK shows being paid, 34.1%, not the three-year average: the FY2025 charge of US$2.1m on profit before tax of US$6.2m is precisely that rate, while the earlier years' single-digit effective rates reflected prior-year adjustments rather than a structural holiday [S3]. Using the lower average would add back roughly a third of the forecast tax bill and flatter both the target and the dividend leg.

The data pack's depreciation figure is the direct-method cash-flow artefact the house warns about, so we restate it from the cost-of-sales note; the restatement multiplies the reported charge by an order of magnitude and is what makes the reported EBITDA comparable with the cash margin [S3]. On capex we deliberately do not carry the last audited year's total into perpetuity. That total is dominated by additions to the stripping activity asset, exploration and evaluation assets and mining properties, which is a mine-development programme together with the one-off terminal and road build, so we hold the sustaining rate at the depreciation rate and treat the balance as development at US$2.1 a tonne [S3] [S2]. We flag the soft spot honestly: the depreciation charge that sets that rate fell by half between the last two audited years, and the notes do not explain the step, so the sustaining rate is a proxy rather than a mine plan [S3]. What the modelled volume step does not need is a new mine. The company's own strategy is to raise the output target inside the existing logistics capacity, so the incremental tonnes ride on fleet and on the annual quota rather than on plant [S2], and the capital actually spent on the haul road, jetty and ports sits as an advance to the logistics affiliate in other non-current assets, not in the capex line at all [S3 note 17]. This is the base case's single optimism and we name it as one rather than bury it: the sustaining-capex rate is below the last audited year's actual, so it raises free cash flow in every forecast year, and it rests on an unexplained depreciation proxy rather than a mine plan. If the last audited year's development rate were the true steady-state rate instead, free cash flow would thin in every forecast year and the value would fall materially — the model's own alternative run puts the DCF and the target several notches lower on that basis, and the assumptions record the numbers. The reader who does not accept the development-versus-sustaining split should take the lower value, not ours.

The balance sheet is levered to the controlling shareholder rather than to banks. Total debt at the last audited date is a non-current shareholder loan, drawn for the first time that year, and the group carried almost no bank debt before it 27.3 USD m [S3]. Liquidity is adequate but not comfortable. Operating cash flow covered capital expenditure in FY2024 — US$15.3m against US$11.1m — but not in FY2025, when US$3.7m of operating cash flow met US$10.0m of capex, so the group part-funded itself through a share placement and shareholder borrowing in the year that the development programme peaked [S3]. Working capital is a modest negative, reflecting contract liabilities from customer advances and payable balances, and the restatement of D&A does not disturb it -2.9.

Earnings quality. The three-year accruals ratio — net profit less operating cash flow over average total assets — is a small negative, roughly minus two-and-a-half per cent, and the year-to-year mix is noisy, so there is no accruals flag here; the volatile element is capitalised stripping and exploration, both legitimate in this industry and disclosed, so we classify them as optics-class rather than manipulation-class [S3] [S0]. The genuine quality issues are structural rather than accounting: related- party concentration on both sides of the P&L, the reliance on shareholder funding, and the volatility of the reported volume series against the smoothness of management's plans [S3] [S2]. On the cost side that concentration is the hauling and jetty logistics routed through the controlling group's affiliate and the marketing fee on the sale side, both set out in the industry section above [S3 note 17, note 29, note 34]. Two more structure points belong here rather than in a footnote. First, the associate is carried above its share of its own net assets — the group's US$25.4m carrying value against a forty-nine per cent share of the associate's US$31.1m of net assets — so an impairment test, not a write-up, is the direction of risk [S3]. Second, the group spent US$41.3m in cash last year buying an intermediate holding company from a counterparty the notes do not list as a related party, part-funded by a placement struck well below today's price [S3] [S2]. The audit is by a firm inside a global network, the opinion is clean, the accounts are in the US dollar, and we found no going-concern language, no special-notation status and no material litigation beyond a nominal administrative sanction for a late auditor appointment [S2] [S3].

The method set is the house coal card: a life-of-asset DCF at through-cycle prices as the primary method, with an EV/EBITDA cross-check and a dividend-capacity cross-check, exactly as the industry card prescribes. A cyclical producer should never be valued on spot earnings or on a current-year multiple, because the current-year multiple embeds the wrong price; the deck's through-cycle marker is the sourced price we underwrite to, and the through-cycle marker is the anchor the whole valuation hangs from.

The cost of capital is built from the macro deck: a US dollar risk-free rate, a mature-market equity risk premium, an Indonesia country risk premium, an unlevered beta, and a small debt weight from the shareholder loan

. Because the company reports in US dollars, no currency premium is added twice; the source of return is the equity risk premium plus the country premium, geared by a levered beta that is barely above the unlevered one because the balance sheet is lightly geared 10.2% 0.84 10.5%.

The primary method discounts the free cash flow to the firm over the licensed window with no terminal value, so the value is the cumulative discounted cash the asset can generate while it is permitted to run

. The producing mine's permit expires in 2030, so the primary DCF stops at the licensed window against a 314 Mt reserve [S2]. The reserve is far larger than that window — 314 Mt against a single-digit-million-tonne annual run-rate — and that is deliberate. This revision re-values it at the sourced strip ratio. FY2026E carries the H1-incurred overburden charge; FY2027E-FY2030E carry the disclosed FY2025 ratio of 2.9 bcm/t [F10] [F4]. That restores positive EBITDA in FY2028E-FY2030E (US$8.3m, US$3.5m and US$5.6m respectively) and moves the value-maximising life end from FY2027E to FY2028E. It does not restore the post-2030 tail: at the deck's through-cycle marker the realised price covers cash cost by a thin margin but does not cover sustaining capital, so on a nominal-consistent path — price and unit costs escalating together at the macro deck's USD inflation, as the industry card requires — the present value of the years beyond the licence is negative. At the extension probabilities the review asks for, half, three-quarters and full extension of a negative number stay non-positive, so the house convention books zero; the breakeven where the extension would pay is a Newcastle marker just above the deck's long-run level. The arithmetic is in the assumptions record. We therefore carry the extension as an unbooked option, not as a bridge item. PP 96/2021 Article 59 still gives a producing IUP Operasi Produksi an extension route, assessed on the holder's performance [S13], and no Triaryani application is on record in the annual report, the FY2025 LK or the H1-2026 LK — we searched all three — but a permit that permits production at a margin below the cost of sustaining capital is not worth paying for in the base case. At the deck's through-cycle marker the calibrated realisation is only a little above the cash cost, which is the whole thesis in one line [d.coal.newc] [S4 note 28]. The extension, and the reserve behind it, pay in the bull price regime; that is where we say so, not in the base value.

The equity bridge subtracts net debt and minority interests and adds back the non-current investments, which is where the associate's carrying value sits, so the associate is not lost inside the single-segment consolidation. That add-back is not free money, and round two was right to test it. The audited carrying value of the forty-nine per cent associate was US$25.4m at the FY2025 audited date and US$24.3m at the latest balance sheet, the figure the cheapest reading of the accounts would add, after a year in which the associate produced nothing at all and its own operating permit lapsed [S3] [S4]. Its own net assets are US$31.1m, so the group carries the stake at a premium to its forty-nine per cent share of the associate's book — the textbook impairment trigger for an asset over an expired licence. We therefore do not carry the expired-licence mine at full book. We mark the stake to its realisable basis — its share of the associate's own net assets — and the mark-down is booked in the bridge, so a reader can see it rather than take it on trust (

). The restart is held as an unbooked option: the mine sold close to a million tonnes two years ago and paid the group a dividend last year [S2] [S3], but a restart that depends on a permit renewal we do not book is upside, not base value, and it is capped at the carrying value we have just written off.

Net debt in the bridge is the reported borrowings less unrestricted cash, with one correction the QC auditor was right to demand. The group drew a short-term bank facility in the first half, and the same balance sheet carries a slightly larger export-proceeds deposit in a restricted account that cannot be withdrawn until that facility is settled [S4 note 17, F45]. The data pack's cash line counts only the unrestricted balance, so deducting the loan without its matched deposit would overstate net debt by about the size of the loan. We net the two, and the separate non-current restricted time deposits are not netted because no facility is matched to them [S4 note 15]. The bridge table below shows every item we book.

The cross-checks disagree with the primary, and we say so. The dividend-capacity method values the name well above the DCF (Rp200, 230.5% above the primary), because it capitalises the modelled twelve-month dividend at the low peer-median yield the coal names carry [S2]. It is a peak-cycle number: it is built on the current-year profit, whose dividend is far above what the through-cycle years support. On the recalibrated cost the later modelled years carry thin or negative net profit — the last two modelled years are losses — so the same yield would imply little or nothing out there, and the current-year profit is the only year that funds a dividend of this size. That is exactly why the leg is a capacity anchor rather than a forecast. We keep it because the coal card requires a dividend-capacity anchor, but we hold it at its configured 15% weight rather than the fifth it would reach if the two remaining legs were simply renormalised, and we disclose the through-cycle value so a reader can see how much of the legacy comes from the cycle [S2 p.101]. The payout behind it is the stated policy midpoint, not a guess; but the company has not paid a dividend for two years and the later modelled years are thin, so it is a capacity anchor, not a forecast. A reader who thinks the board keeps the dividend at zero should take the DCF alone as the value.

The EV/EBITDA cross-check is absent for a dull reason: it drops out because the data pack's trailing period carries no EBITDA field, so the metric cannot be computed at all — not because the metric is negative [S0]. That omission lowers the blended value relative to a three-method result, because the forward multiple is richer than the DCF; we state the direction rather than let the gap look neutral. The shares trade on 22.0x of our forecast EBITDA, which is itself a warning about the price, but it is not the reason the method is missing.

On realisation the method is deliberate rather than inherited. The calibrated ratio keys off the seaborne Newcastle marker because that is the reviewed series the whole coal peer set in this book uses and the low-rank index markers are not reviewable in the deck; the rank discount sits inside the calibrated ratio, cross-checked against the deck's own mid- and low-calorie reference prices for this rank [d.coal.newc] [d.coal.hba_ii]. Sensitivity to the benchmark price and to the rupiah is wide, and the bear and bull outcomes span a very large range, which is the honest shape of a marginal mine whose cash margin is thin in the current year and thinner still at the deck's through-cycle price, where it does not cover sustaining capital

What the price implies is the most useful number in this report. To justify today's price on our own DCF, the seaborne benchmark would have to run at a multiple of the deck's forward path US$339/t 2.9. That is a statement about the war premium persisting, not about this company's execution. On the trailing multiples the shares have changed hands on a triple-digit multiple of trailing earnings and on a low-double-digit multiple of book 127.8x 16.1x, with the forward multiple only coming down sharply if the deck's current-year price and a volume recovery land together 46.7x.

The coal card asks for four anchors the last draft left out, and we add them with their limits. First, NAV at spot: the deck's spot print of US$150/t sits about a tenth above the current-year path, and the sensitivity table shows that even at a benchmark a tenth higher the DCF remains a fraction of the quoted price — spot is cycle position, not a different company [d.coal.newc]. Second, the cost-curve quartile: we do not have a licensed global cash-cost curve in the registry and will not invent one, so we cannot place the mine in a quartile; what we can source is that its ex-royalty cash cost of US$30.0 a tonne is roughly half the HBA II marker of US$66.1/t for this grade, which is the signature of a high-cost producer, not a first-quartile one [d.coal.hba_ii] [S3]. Third, EV/reserves: at the current market capitalisation the enterprise value is a couple of dollars per reserve tonne against the 314 Mt reserve [S0] [S2]. Fourth, the trough years now carry a thin positive EBITDA rather than the loss the previous draft showed — US$8.3m falling to US$3.5m — against which net debt is 1.9x; that is a meaningful but uncomfortable multiple, and it says the balance sheet is carried by a year that barely covers its cost of capital. The trough loss shows at the net-profit and free-cash-flow lines, not at EBITDA. The shares pay a forward yield of 0.5% against the peer-median yield the dividend leg uses, so the market is plainly not using the dividend anchor here — it is pricing the option on the benchmark, which is what the reverse DCF above says.

The konglo lens is the final step, and it is why the target is not the fundamental value. The business valuation above — the probability-weighted blend of the life-of-asset DCF and the dividend-capacity cross-check — gives a fundamental twelve-month value of Rp180. The market does not trade there: at Rp2,750 the shares sit at 15.2 times that value, a log premium of 2.7. The konglo deck's regime reads that gap as a float and index fact rather than a fundamental one, and the lens, not the analyst, sets how much of it persists. Over the deck's three regime scenarios the twelve-month price keeps part of today's premium, target = fundamental value times (price / value) raised to one minus c, where c is the share of the log gap closed: c is 0.4 in the base regime, raised above the deck's own 0.3 by this name's two regime flags — the HSC listing and the free-float step due inside the window, which add 0.1 together [S7] [S8]. The HSC flag is now effective rather than prospective: the exclusion from the IHSG calculation applies from 2 November 2026, with the shares still listed and tradeable [S14] [S15]. We do not raise c on that account. The overlay already prices the HSC status, and an exclusion date tells us when index demand stops, not that the price converges on fundamental value faster than the deck's own curve; lifting c further would be an unsourced acceleration of the regime, not a consequence of the event [S14]. Deeper compression in the bear regime (c 0.8) and a premium that widens rather than closes in the bull regime (the deck's bull setting plus this name's two flags, which leaves the engine's compress at a small negative) give the three regime outcomes in

. The result is a target of Rp1,323 against a price of Rp2,750, a total return of -51.4%. We are explicit about what that is and is not: it is a statement about the regime, not about the asset, and the fundamental value it multiplies is the one built above, Rp180.

We are equally explicit about why the base regime, not the bear regime, is the most likely path — the red team is right that the earlier draft's reason was wrong. The float step and the MSCI decision both fall inside the twelve-month window, so the index and float treatment *can* change inside it; the question is only how much of the log gap the regime closes in that time, not whether the tape is stable. The deck's compress curve takes 0.4 of the log gap in twelve months, raised above the deck's own base by this name's two flags — the HSC listing and the dated free-float step — which together add 0.1 [S7] [S8]. That produces a base thirty regime value of Rp922, roughly Rp310 in the bear regime (c 0.8) and Rp3,138 in the bull regime (the deck's bull setting plus this name's two flags, so the premium widens slightly). We do not raise the base compress further for one reason: the free-float rule needs the float to move from the annual report's 11.6% to 12.5%, a gap of just under a percentage point, but that gap is not small in flow terms. It is about thirty-four million shares — roughly a tenth of the free float — which at today's price is more than a hundred billion rupiah, or around six weeks of the name's entire average daily turnover [S8] [S0]. That is the single most likely supply event in the window, and there are two mechanisms: a market sell-down by the controller, which is the bear path, or a discounted placement, which is dilutive but cash-raising and is what the company did in 2025 at a price far below today's [S2]. Both effects are already inside the small premium the lens adds for the step; a deeper base compress would require evidence that the premium closes faster than the deck's own curve, and we do not have it. We also searched the annual report and the LK for pledged controller shares and found no disclosure that the controlling stake is pledged — the AR records only that no board member held shares directly or filed a pledge report [S2 p.153] — so we cannot evidence a margin-call channel, but we cannot rule one out either.

The clearest way to lose money here on the long side is to be right about coal and wrong about this company. The realised price is a fraction of the benchmark, so a strong benchmark lifts a small absolute margin; the haul, barge and jetty charges are largely fixed per tonne, so a volume shortfall spreads them over fewer tonnes; and the annual quota is set by the government, not by the company. A downward revision to the RKAB, a further multi-year delay in the associate's restart, or a prolonged wet season that closes the haul road would each compress the margin well before the seaborne price moved [S2] [S6]. The licence clock is a risk in its own right: the producing mine's permit runs out at the end of the decade and the associate's has already lapsed, and any production beyond 2030 needs an extension the government grants at its discretion [S13]. That tail is not in the base value at all: at the recalibrated cost the reserve does not cover the cost of sustaining capital at the deck's through-cycle price, so a refusal costs the base case nothing and an extension adds value only in the bull price regime, where it is the largest single upside we can name.

Regulatory risk is the highest-impact item: royalty rates, the domestic market obligation, export proceeds retention and quota administration are all live policy levers, and they bite hardest on the marginal producer. Macro risk is second: the deck itself flags that spot sits well above its forward path as a war-premium carry, so a normalisation of that premium is a direct hit to the value we underwrite to. Currency risk is modest and runs the other way: the company earns in dollars and reports in dollars, so a weaker rupiah flatters the rupiah share price without changing the economics. Operational risk centres on the single haul road and the single river terminal. Governance risk is real and specific — revenue concentration in a related party, a controlling shareholder above two-thirds of the register, a very small free float and a controlling stake that makes the tape thin and volatile, as the suspension showed. The konglo regime is the market expression of that concentration: the HSC exclusion removes index demand from 2 November 2026 [S14] and the free-float deadline forces an ownership step-down inside the window, and either can move the price far more than a quarter's earnings [S8] [S7]. Liquidity risk for us is minimal: the name trades a large enough daily value to enter and exit.

Those are the business scenarios, and they are separate from the konglo regime scenarios the lens runs. The regime set does not shock the coal price; it shocks how much of the market's premium the float and the index rules keep over the coming year. In the bear regime the gap closes 0.8 of the way to fundamental value and the shares are worth Rp310; in the base regime, which closes 0.4, they are worth Rp922; in the bull regime the premium widens rather than closes (the deck's bull setting plus this name's two flags) and they are worth Rp3,138. Those three are what the lens blends into the Rp1,323 target, and they are the reason the target sits above the fundamental value even on a SELL call.

The regime catalysts carry dates and they are the ones to diarise. The exchange's free-float rule requires the float to reach 12.5% by 31 March 2027 and the full floor by 31 March 2028, from 11.5% today — a gap of 1.0% to the first step, about 4.9 months out — so a placement or a controller sell-down into the public float is the single most likely flow event in the window, and it is the mechanism that would close the premium fastest [S8]. MSCI opened its consultation on moving Indonesia to Standalone status on 15 October 2026, with feedback to 30 April 2027 and a decision by 30 June 2027; a Standalone outcome would cut the passive demand that partly supports a name like this one [S9]. The HSC exclusion from the IHSG calculation is effective from Monday 2 November 2026 and the list is reviewed quarterly, so index-tracking demand for the name ends at the open and is re-tested at each review [S14] [S15]. The exclusion is a flow event, not a delisting: the shares stay listed and tradeable [S15]. A change of control would be the other dated event: if the controller ever sold its stake it would trigger a mandatory tender offer, and the group's own capital-markets agenda — a rights issue, an asset injection, an IPO of a sibling — is the standard way a konglo float step is delivered.

Bear case — the benchmark mean-reverts faster than the deck as Chinese output restarts and Indonesian supply returns; the quota plus a soft first half leave volume a little light; and the realised ratio gives back a tenth as the sales mix and grade slip. That give-back is the mirror of the bull's upgrade, not a claim about the related party: the GCI contract discloses no price, so we cannot say whether it is above or below delivered market [S3 note 27/34]. Free cash flow thins, neither the shareholder loan nor the short-term bank loan is repaid and the dividend stays at zero, and at the trough through-cycle price the mine covers its recalibrated cash cost only barely and does not cover sustaining capital. Base case — the deck path is broadly right: the benchmark steps down through the middle of the decade to its long-run level, volume recovers modestly from the current run-rate, and the current year, priced near spot, is the only year that carries a solid cash margin; at the deck's through-cycle level the margin is thin and below the cost of sustaining capital, so the life DCF ends inside the licensed window and the dividend is a first-year capacity anchor rather than a stream. Bull case — the war premium holds, the Indonesian supply-discipline bid keeps the benchmark above the deck, the quota is lifted toward the company's own plan, the realised ratio upgrades a tenth as the sales mix widens beyond the single related party, and volume rises, so the margin expands and the value re-rates. The bull's upgrade would also capture an arm's-length repricing if the undisclosed contract price proves to be at or below delivered market, but with no disclosed price we cannot size that on top of the mirrored shock. Probabilities are set at the house default with the base case above 0.5.

We keep the scenarios honest in both directions. The three upside events the earlier draft named in the bull narrative — an associate restart, a licence renewal past 2030 and a haulage-cost relief — are no longer asserted as scenario outcomes because the shocks do not carry them: the licence tail is not booked in the base at all, so it cannot be double-counted; the associate restart is an unbooked option; and a haulage cost relief has no sourced US$/t figure, so it belongs in the signposts below, not in a shock we cannot source. What the bull case does carry is the two things the base case holds fixed — the benchmark and the realised price — lifted together with volume, which is the honest shape of the upside for a price-taker.

Signposts that would change our view: an RKAB quota materially above the current run-rate; a renewal of the producing mine's operating licence past the end of the decade together with a benchmark that keeps the realised price above the level that covers sustaining capital, which is when the reserve tail would be worth booking; a restart date for the associate's East Kalimantan mine; a sourced haulage cost per tonne falling below the last audited level; a sustained benchmark above the deck's forward path for more than a quarter; and any step-change in the related-party share of revenue.

The register is concentrated and the float is thin. The controlling shareholder is a holding company of a Singapore-listed coal group that became the controlling shareholder in this century's twenties, and the ultimate beneficial owners are named individuals; the second-largest holder is an affiliated entity, and public shareholders hold a low-double-digit share 11.5% 88.4% [S2]. Members of the board hold no direct shares but hold indirect interests through the controlling structure [S2].

SMMT is a konglo name in the regime sense, and it is worth naming the entities precisely because the regime now turns on them. The controlling shareholder is PT Geo Energy Investama, a subsidiary of Geo Energy Resources Limited, which is listed on the mainboard of the Singapore Exchange; it became the controlling shareholder in 2023, taking the stake from the Rajawali group's PT Mutiara Timur Pratama [S2 p.46-47]. On the annual report's own share-ownership chart the controller and the second holder, PT Golden Prima Energy, hold 88.4% of the register between them, so the public float is only 11.6% [S2 p.45]. The data pack and the house registry carry a slightly lower figure, and our konglo lens uses the registry's, so the gap to the first statutory step is just under a percentage point rather than a full point; the two bases should be reconciled, and we flag that for the Director rather than pick the flattering one [S2 p.45, p.64]. The float sits below the exchange's new statutory floor, and the name is in the market-capitalisation tier whose first step is 12.5% by 31 March 2027 and the full floor by 31 March 2028 — roughly 4.9 months away [S8]. The exchange placed SMMT on its high-shareholding-concentration list as of 22 October 2026 [S7], and the HSC exclusion from the IHSG calculation becomes effective on 2 November 2026 [S14]; the excluded shares remain listed and tradeable [S15]. We do not extend that to the LQ45, IDX30 or IDX80: the house registry carries the wider bar, but no exchange or index announcement we have found places SMMT outside those indices, and the exchange's simultaneous review changed other constituents without naming SMMT [S15] — absence of mention is not evidence of exclusion. We therefore treat the IHSG exclusion as the sourced flow fact and record the wider index bar as an unverified registry field for the Director to fix [S15]. Nor do we have a source placing SMMT outside the MSCI indices: the May MSCI deletions were large konglo names, not this one [S11]. The registry records no OJK enforcement finding against this name and no index deletion for it [S11]. On pledged shares we checked the annual report's ownership and share-pledge disclosure and the LK: neither discloses a pledge over the controlling stake (the AR records only that no director or commissioner held shares directly and that no such pledge report was filed) [S2 p.153]. That is "none disclosed — checked", not "none exists", and the thin float plus the group's own borrowing means a margin-call channel cannot be ruled out. One registry gap we record rather than paper over: the house konglo registry carries no group label for this name, so the group row of the profile table below renders empty even though the controller is named on the annual report's own ownership page [S2 p.46-47]. The controlling entity is PT Geo Energy Investama, a subsidiary of SGX-listed Geo Energy Resources Limited, and the correct group label is that Singapore group; we flag the empty registry field for the Director to fix rather than assert a group the registry does not carry. On group consistency there is nothing to mark but the fundamentals: the controlling group's listed vehicle, Geo Energy Resources, trades in Singapore and is not a covered name in this book, so there is no covered listed sibling to carry into a sum-of-the-parts at house value, and the value we hold is the one built in the valuation section above.

Two corporate actions in the last audited year are structure flags under the house earnings-quality screen, and round one mentioned them without assessing them. First, the company issued new shares totalling 275 m shares with no pre-emptive rights, for IDR220.0bn — an implied price of roughly a quarter of today's Rp2,750 — which is dilutive to public holders as a matter of arithmetic even though it was disclosed and approved [S2]. Second, it paid US$41.3m in cash for a hundred per cent of an intermediate holding company, PT Bara Enim Sejahtera, whose disclosed total assets at the year-end were a fraction of that price [S3] [S2]. The counterparty, PT Sinar Unggul Internasional, is not among the related parties the notes list, so we do not call it a related-party deal [S3]; but the price paid over the acquired book, funded partly by a placement struck far below the current market, is exactly the per-share-value-leak pattern the screen looks for, and we say so rather than bury it. Neither flag changes the rating on its own; both are reasons to hold the governance discount we already apply.

Related-party gravity is the central governance fact and the reason we would discount any related-party-derived revenue in a stress case. A very large share of the group's coal revenue is a sale to a single affiliate of the controlling shareholder under a coal sales and purchase agreement, with a marketing-services agreement alongside it, and the counterparty also holds the contract liability that funds part of the working capital 77.4 USD m [S3]. The borrowings are a related-party shareholder loan, which the group both borrows from and services inside the family of companies, plus a short-term bank loan of US$11.0m first drawn in the first half of 2026 (27.3 USD m and 11.0 USD m) [S3] [S4]. This is the modal Indonesian value-destruction channel, and while the arrangement is disclosed and carries no adverse finding, it means the realised price we calibrate to is itself a related-party price, which is a limitation on our evidence we state plainly. The bear case gives back a tenth of the realised ratio on a mix and grade slip, and the valuation is sensitive to it because the whole ratio comes off this contract [S3]. We do not claim the direction of the related-party price against market: no price is disclosed, so an arm's-length repricing could sit on either side, and the bull case carries the upgrade that would capture it if the contract proves to be at or below delivered market [S3 note 27/34].

The audit is clean and by a firm within a global network; the opinion is unqualified; there is no going-concern paragraph; and the only sanction disclosed is a nominal administrative penalty for a late auditor appointment in an earlier year [S2] [S3]. There is no material litigation, no special-monitoring-board status and no special-notation letter, so the IDX regime gate is clear [S2].

On the dividend record the company paid nothing in either of the last two audited years, having paid interim dividends earlier in the decade; the stated policy is a fixed share of net profit after tax within a band, subject to the general meeting, so dividend capacity exists but has not recently been exercised [S2]. On ESG, the exposures that matter are the energy transition — which management itself names as its central challenge and to which it responds with fleet electrification and operational efficiency rather than any change in the product — plus mine rehabilitation, acid mine drainage and mine-closure provisioning, all of which are disclosed and provisioned in the accounts [S2] [S3].

The dated catalysts are the quarterly filings, the annual quota decision and the audited statements. The next quarterly report is the first hard read on whether the volume recovery after the late quota issuance is real, and the quota decision for the coming year sets the volume ceiling under which the whole plan operates [S3] [S6]. The audited statements will test the company's own revenue target against what was actually realised — a test the annual report itself answers inconsistently for the last audited year, reporting the revenue plan met at about half in one section while its structured target table shows the volume target reached [S2] — so the printed actual is the number we watch, not the achievement percentage in the prose.

To the operational list we add the licence clock and the regime events. The licence clock is now a date to diarise rather than a cliff: the producing mine's permit expires in 2030 and the associate's has already lapsed, and PP 96/2021 lets a holder apply for an extension five to one-and-a-half years before expiry, assessed on performance [S13]. No Triaryani extension application is on record in the annual report, the FY2025 LK or the H1-2026 LK, so it is the filing itself — not a decision we can assume — that is the event to watch; the directorate's decision would re-open the tail we currently leave unbooked, but only at a benchmark that lifts the realised price above the level that covers sustaining capital. The regime events are dated and independent of the coal price: the free-float step to 12.5% by 31 March 2027, the quarterly HSC reviews after the IHSG exclusion took effect on 2 November 2026, the MSCI consultation decision by 30 June 2027, and any group corporate action by the controller — a placement, a sell-down or an asset injection — that delivers the float [S8] [S9]. We watch the monthly shareholder registry for any change in the ownership chart and for a change of control, which would trigger a mandatory tender offer.

Between updates we watch a short list of KPIs: the realised price per tonne against the low-calorie reference series; the RKAB quota and any revision; the split of sales between export and domestic, since the domestic mix caps the price; the related-party share of revenue; the haulage cost per tonne, which is the single largest cost line; the strip ratio and overburden volume; the capex-versus-development split, so we can tell when the terminal build is finished; and the debt structure at the latest balance sheet, where the shareholder loan and a first short-term bank loan sit together, the shareholder loan being the larger and the family-serviced line [S3] [S4] [S2].

Our monitoring is deliberately built around the physical bottlenecks rather than around the coal
price alone, because for a producer of this rank the price is a market fact and the logistics are a
company fact. The two things that would make us revisit the rating upward are a sustained rise in
the realised price relative to the benchmark and evidence that the terminal build is complete, either
of which would raise the cash margin without needing us to change our view of the cycle.
